utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Please proceed to call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you too. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Anna Richterova, assisted by Hasan Younis, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Milan Trbojevic. I'm with the lead counsel John Ackerman and our assistant Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Appearance for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you. Preliminaries? Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to say that this morning I was able to have a productive meeting with counsel for General Talic, which I hope will shorten matters both today and at a later stage. Mr. Ackerman on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin wasn't there, but as I understand it, because he was in agreement with the general principles that we discussed. The first was this: Your Honour will recall that yesterday at the end of the evidence in chief of this witness, Mr. Ackerman said that he didn't think he was going to cross-examine and there was some discussion between General Talic and his counsel. I was asked today whether I would be prepared to make some admissions in relation to this particular incident and Kljuc generally. And I'm happy so to do and in a moment I'll hand a copy to Your Honours and read it into the record, because it will certainly shorten matters with this witness. One of the matters we discussed was this question of where witnesses give evidence where the actual facts cannot be disputed by the defendants because it's not suggested -- the accused, I'm sorry -- that either of them were there. And whether it was necessary for these people to come and give evidence, unless for some reason the Prosecution thought that they would assist. And again, I'm happy to say, and I think it's in the interests of all parties, particularly the accused, that a general agreement was reached that when the list of witnesses for a municipality is given out in advance, the Defence will notify us if they do not require to cross-examine a particular witness. And on some occasions it may be if the Prosecution is prepared to make various admissions about those events. So that is, I think, something that we've achieved even without a Status Conference, as it were. Your Honour, in relation therefore to this incident, the killings at the Biljani school, can I hand to Your Honours and an original to the Court -- and I have other copies available for other interested parties. And I'm sorry, I've forgotten to give it to the interpreters. But I don't think it matters, because it's very short, although if they want it, we can hand it in before I read it out. There are three copies for Your Honours. And the original -- I hope it's the original, for the Court. I think it probably ought to be given an exhibit number, which by our reckoning is Exhibit 1078. I haven't got my earphones on, so I don't know whether the interpreters want to be given a copy quickly. They do or they don't?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If necessary. If it's going to be used, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry? Forgive me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm told, Your Honour, they're going to be the intervening numbers which have not yet been used up will be used up by Ms. Richterova today. So we'd ask that that be marked Exhibit 1078. Your Honour, not having heard a request through my earphones -- well, I may have, because I haven't got them -- sorry. All right. I'm sorry. Now I've got the earphones plugged in. Do the interpreters want a copy before I read this out?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the document is going to be used, it would be useful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour I'm told it would be. Can I hand out copies to the interpreters. If somebody could just hand them in to the booth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the -- the copies will be coming. I see the interpreters -- I think the usher has gone round to the wrong booth, but any how -- if I read it very slowly. And both Defence counsel have got copies. It's headed "Admission." And I've put number 1 in, because I anticipate there will be more to come, Your Honour -- made on behalf of the Prosecutor. 1: Documents indicate that on or about the 6th of June 1992, the majority of the municipality of Kljuc was transferred from the area of responsibility ("AOR") of the 1st Krajina Corps to that of the 2nd Krajina Corps. 2: Units of the 1st Krajina Corps continued to operate in Kljuc after that date and Momir Talic continued to report on events in that municipality. 3: Marko Samardzija, who (according to witnesses) was in charge of the troops who carried out the massacre of the Biljani school on the 10th of July 1992, came within the authority of the 2nd Krajina Corps. Your Honour, I hope that is self-explanatory. Your Honour, in due course, the whole area of responsibilities will be explained by the witness Ewan Brown whose report we hope to be able to disclose very shortly. Your, may I also add this in relation to the witnesses today and tomorrow and for the rest of this week: Because of the break, none of the witnesses arrived here except for the one that Ms. Richterova -- the two that Ms. Richterova has been calling -- will call until yesterday evening. As a result, what we would ask Your Honours to do, even if we run a bit short or stop early today, is the next witness who's going to deal with the massacre at Velagici will be starting tomorrow he's been seen today by the lawyer Mr. Nicholls calling him. And if that again runs short, the next witness who I shall be calling -- and I can't remember whether he requires protective measures, so can I -- I think Your Honour has been notified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think he does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's 7. -- I had the papers this morning. The third one is 7.65. And he is required -- is it BT26?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It's -- yes, he will be giving evidence tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, that's tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's tomorrow. 7.133 will give evidence directly after this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then 7.105, who as I say will be dealing with the overall picture of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. That is not a protective witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, he's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The one before him, 7.65, BT26.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. Your Honour, he is at the moment -- he's here, but he's going through documents. The problem with him is there is a gentleman with exactly the same name but who comes from a different area. And our searches have thrown up the documents relating to the other gentleman as well. So he's at the moment having to go through to sort out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the other gentleman was born in Kljuc. Yes? And he did mention a brother of his was coming over to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. I think Your Honour -- Your Honour is misunderstanding. There's a man with exactly the same name as Witness 7.105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I was referring to someone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. We gathered together -- we discovered a whole lot of documents that related to the other man. And so it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's quite an exercise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's like me and the footballer, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so Your Honour, that is why we ask not to call him until Thursday. So that's the situation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also the Registrar -- I've asked the Registrar to approach you with a view to informing you that in all probability, Friday we will need to -- we will require to start a little bit late.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the other thing I was going to come to, which is my personal difficulties yet again. There's a Status Conference listed in the cases of Gruban and Fustar, Banovic, and others. It's the Keraterm, Omarska case. And at the moment, I have the -- the control of those cases as well. I hope for not too much longer. We've asked -- it's listed in this court, Court I -- well, no. Well, it's listed before the Trial Chamber that normally sits in Court I. I don't know which court they would be in. I've attempted to ask the legal officer who's dealing with it if it could be listed at 12.30 when Milosevic finishes. I've not yet had an answer. At the moment the suggestion is it may be during the course of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would suit me fine, because what is happening is the President of Malta is coming over. And I've been asked to join him. Unfortunately I'm not in a position to say no, although I will try to come here as quickly as I can. There's certain protocol that has to be observed, and I don't anticipate to be here before 3.00. I mean, that's -- that's the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I -- that would be most helpful, Your Honour. In fact, if we could try -- and perhaps the two Trial Chambers could try and liaise. Because if they could list the Status Conference, say, at 2.00, that would suit everybody perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was his mentor. He was my ex-professor of criminal law. And we've worked together hand in hand until he was made Minister of Justice for some time back and then President of the Republic, and we have remained on very good terms. So I could -- I really couldn't escape -- escape this. So that's -- that's the situation as Friday is concerned. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that may, as I say, well assist. So that's the general timetable then for this week. And may I ask, Your Honour -- I'll just stay for the end of this witness. But would Your Honour forgive me then if I leave court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because I have another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Now, is there going to be a cross-examination of yesterday's witness? Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Brdjanin, we have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. And Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, we will have -- we believe, 45 minutes of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we'll admit the witness once more into the courtroom, please. Thank you. You have had time to consult your client and yourself, I understand. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure he has had time to consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That has resulted with the admission of the--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I anticipated that much, because although I don't understand the language, I could understand more or less what he was saying yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are concluding today with your evidence, and you will be cross-examined by one of the Defence teams. You will not be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: before we proceed, may I ask you to repeat the solemn declaration that you made yesterday, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. The Defence team for Radoslav Brdjanin have no questions to put to you. The Defence team for General Talic have got a few questions to put to you. Again, I recommend to you, give you the same advice as I gave you yesterday, to be brief in your answers and to be precise in your answers, trying to answer the question and nothing but the question. Mr. Zecevic is the lead counsel for General Talic, and he is going to be the one to cross-examine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Cajic.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Slobodan Zecevic, and I'm going to put a few questions to you.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cajic, up to now you have given four statements; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You gave those statements to the security service in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993, 1994, and 1997.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And to the investigators of the Prosecution in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Cajic, try to allow just a very short interval between question and answer and question so that the interpreters can catch up with you, because since you both speak the same language, the same problem that arises when we are all speaking English repeats itself. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cajic, you left Kljuc around September 1992.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 19th or the 20th. I'm not sure. The 21st perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you left Kljuc, you went to Travnik; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After you had arrived in Travnik, you joined the BH army; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I had nowhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you join immediately, or how much time passed after you joined the BH army when you arrived in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined immediately, since I was registered there. But I rested for a few months and I continued with work in the working platoon in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you say you were registered, from what date were you registered there?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that I was -- since the collection centre was in the barracks in Travnik, I think that from the day I arrived in Travnik, I was registered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me yesterday you said that for a certain period of time you hid together with Mr. Dzaferagic.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Semso Dzaferagic, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did he join the BH army too?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that for one year he was absent -- he was in Zenica and Kakanj. He had psychological problems, so he wasn't present. But he was in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to 1992. Yesterday you spoke about a checkpoint in front of Sanica.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the bridge, to be precise, the bridge over the River Sanica, in front of the entrance to Sanica, 500 or 600 metres from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were -- that people were checked at that checkpoint going in both directions, their identity papers were checked.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Their papers were checked after the takeover on the 21st, after the mixed police had taken over, when just one -- when the team was composed of just one nationality, that's when they started checking the papers. Up until that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, isn't it correct to say that the police always had the right to check the papers of citizens at any time, regardless of the nationality of the police?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And yesterday I mentioned this. But given that my sister-in-law and my brother worked in the factory in Sanica and a day or two later -- I don't know whether they carried on going to work. But colleagues, neighbours with whom they had grown up checked the papers of my sister-in-law or of my brother. Given that there was -- there was no need to do this, because they had known each other for about 20 years or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I only asked you whether it was normal for the police to check the papers of citizens. Was this part of their authority?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case everywhere in the world. It's normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Cajic, you served in the army; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After you had finished your military service, did you participate in some sort of reservist exercise?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember - and if you didn't, did men of yours with whom you participated in those trainings, training exercises - did these men receive some sort of compensation if they were employed in a company?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. If it lasted for several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If in 1992 you had responded to the mobilisation, you, too, would have been remunerated; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cajic, we've mentioned these checkpoints which were set up in 1992. You remember that in your statement given in the year 2000 to the investigators for the Prosecution, in that statement you said that those checkpoints hadn't been erected at the main roads and we didn't have any difficulties.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not until mid-March. There were no checkpoints up until then. And then in the middle of March 1992, the checkpoints were set up and they remained there until I left my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I read out a sentence from your statement which you gave to investigators in the year 2000 and in which you said that you didn't have any difficulties on account of these checkpoints. And yesterday you said that you even had to ask for some sort of authorisation in order to cut the grass in your meadow.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, I said we didn't have any difficulties when there were checkpoints, up until the 20th of May. After the 20th of May, when people were sent back, people who worked in the factory and who were of Muslim nationality, from that date onwards all the problems started, all the problems that arose in Sanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These problems, did they occur after the ambushes that occurred in Pudin Han and Krasulje?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear about this event, but because I was -- I lived 7 to 10 kilometres away from the spot, I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you also indicated, when you spoke about these checkpoints, that -- I am referring to the sentence -- one sentence before the one that I just quoted. There was a war going on in Croatia, and because of the differences in the opinions between Croats and Serbs in the village, it seems that Serbs were taking up measures in order to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I have used the words "in order to protect themselves."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... supplied the witness with his statement from 2000 -- 30th of June, 2000 in Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have the references, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, 3rd of June. Sorry. 3rd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cajic, you will find it on page 3 of your statement, the last and the one before last -- the two last sentences; page 4 of the English version for the Court.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're correct. But I think that this was misinterpreted when my statement was being recorded, because they had no one to protect themselves from. While the war was still going on from Croatia, there was no need for them to protect themselves. Bosnia was still peaceful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that you had seen helicopters coming to the hamlet of Gologlavo in 1992.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw helicopters on several occasions. My house is located below the Gologlavo Brdo, some 1000 metres from the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was in 1992, sometime in April or March. I'm not sure about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and have a look at the statement on the same page, paragraph 3 from the top, starting with the words "during 1991." Have you found that quotation?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "During 1991, I saw military helicopters landing in the Serb hamlet of Gologlavo."

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. No problem. There may have been a mistake. You know, sometimes when you have a lot of things to say, it can be very confusing. And because at the time I worked in Bravsko, I was very close to the main road. And while I was giving my statement, I probably indicated everything that I had seen. So that is how this piece of information remained in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly that you stand by your statement that you had seen these helicopters in 1991?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not going to commit myself either way, 1991 or 1992, because a lot of things occurred during that period of time just prior and leading up to the outbreak of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well then. Witness, a moment ago in response to one of my questions in relation to your statement, you told us that local Serbs did not have to protect themselves from their fellow citizens, members of other ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that in Biljani, in the village of Brkici, Muslims had militarily organised themselves in early 1991?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Mr. Avdic Amir and then Alem Mujezinovic were the first commanders of a military unit which consisted of four companies from Biljani -- three companies from Biljani?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gentleman in question lived in the area of Kljuc. He was not in Biljani. Alem Mujezinovic, on the other hand, lived some seven or eight hundred metres away from my house, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that Alem Mujezinovic was the commander of this unit?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that Smail Domazet was the commander of the platoon in Domazeti?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about Zijad Avdic, do you know that he was the commander of the platoon in Brkici?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please. Your late brother, Ale Cajic --

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not my brother. He was my cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your cousin. Are you aware of the fact that he was the commander of a detachment -- of the local detachment in Brkici?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know the leader of the Sanica Crisis Staff, Selman Mujaga?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Privately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was the leader of the Sanica Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the order dated 6th of May, 1992 regarding the prevention of movement of the military and the police in Muslim villages which was issued by the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: War Staff of Bosanski Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that sometime around the 1st of June, if I understood you correctly, the hamlet in which you lived at the time was searched by the military for the first time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that you had heard that Hamdo Cehic was killed on that day.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. When they came on the first occasion -- well, they came back three days later. And it was on the first occasion that Hamdo Cehic was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't you hear that a soldier was killed by a sniper on the same day?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. But I did hear that one of the soldiers was taken away in a van in the village of Cehici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mean that he was wounded. He was taken away because he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that was on the same day.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I also believe that I stated yesterday in my testimony that I was personally present when the platoon commander told us that we should stop the fire from that location. And then we told him, "Well, that's your observation point. That's where the fire is coming from." And several minutes later when the communication was established, all activity stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The soldier in question was a Serb, was he not?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in one more thing which remains to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us about Mladjo Tesic.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was some sort of deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about the same Mladjo Tesic who subsequently helped you reach Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not trying to hide the fact. He personally took me to Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mladjo Tesic from before?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So Mladjo Tesic was the deputy commander when this event happened in Biljani. And two months later he helped you reach Kljuc, so that you could continue further to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, there's no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Cajic, that brings us to an end. That concludes your -- that concludes your evidence here. And before you are escorted out of this courtroom back to where you're staying and then taken care of and repatriated, it is my duty here on behalf of the other two Judges and myself and the rest of the Tribunal to thank you for having come over and to give evidence in this case. You will be taken care of by the persons responsible for you. And once more, before you leave, I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the other witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, the other witness should be ready in the waiting room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And he was granted closed session and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. We have to wait for the usher, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honour will forgive me, I'll leave the rest of the proceeds to Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We're talking of 7.133, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: BT25. And you expect to conclude with this witness today?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I am -- my intention is to focus only on the incident itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Usher, please the next witness is a protected one, and it will be a closed session. So could I kindly ask you to prepare the courtroom for that purpose, please. Thank you. Yeah. We'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 4.50 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday the 28th day of August, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 25
